block.semiconductor-lab.solar_cell.note1: A silicon panel that turns sunlight straight into electricity. The goal of chapter 2!
block.semiconductor-lab.solar_cell.note2: p-n junction slices 8 + copper cable. Gives 60 W in daytime under open sky (glass is fine), about 12 W (20%) on rainy, cloudy days from scattered light, and 0 at night or under a roof. Right-click to see the output. Connect with copper cable like other generators. The real 1954 cell had an arsenic-doped n-type base (the game uses phosphorus).
block.semiconductor-lab.solar_cell.note3: Noon sunlight is about 1000 W per m². With 6% efficiency, a 1 m² block gives 60 W. In 1954 Bell Labs said its cells could deliver about 50 W per square yard, which matches.
block.semiconductor-lab.solar_cell.note4: On 25 April 1954 Chapin, Fuller and Pearson showed the 'Bell Solar Battery' running a toy Ferris wheel. The 1954 cell used a dull plastic film to stop reflection, and both contacts were on the back. In 1958 cells powered the satellite Vanguard 1. Today's home panels reach over 20%.
block.semiconductor-lab.solar_cell.place: Approximation: output does not change with the sun's height or cloud thickness (only day/night and rain; rain = 20% ⚠️, real overcast light varies). The n-type base is phosphorus, not arsenic as in 1954 ⚠️. Electrodes are copper cable (the 1954 electrode metal is not yet checked ⚠️). Reflection coating omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.silvered_plate.no: A copper plate faced with silver and polished like a mirror.
Copper ingot + silver nugget. Held over iodine vapor it becomes a sensitized plate.
Daguerreotypes often used 'Sheffield plate', copper bonded with silver. Any haze on the surface clouded the image.
The image forms on the silver surface itself, so it had to be flat and clean: plates were polished many times and finally cleaned with acid.
item.semiconductor-lab.daguerreotype_pla: A silver plate given a golden film by iodine vapor. Light makes an invisible image on it. ⚠ Handle in the dark.
Silvered copper plate + iodine. Hold it in the hand opposite the camera and expose it with the camera.
Daguerre held the silver plate over iodine vapor, turning its surface into a thin silver iodide (AgI) film. He judged the right thickness by the film's color changing from gold to violet.
Around 1841, adding bromine vapor after iodine multiplied the sensitivity and cut exposures from minutes to tens of seconds, which made portraits possible.
item.semiconductor-lab.camera.note1: A dark box with a lens. Light from the scene falls on the plate inside and makes a photograph.
item.semiconductor-lab.camera.note2: Achromatic lens + 4 planks. Hold a sensitized plate in your other hand; the shutter is open while you hold right-click. Under open daytime sky a silver plate (daguerreotype) needs 60 s and a gelatin dry plate 1 s (rain gives 30% light; under a roof or at night nothing). Too short is 'thin', too long is 'dark'.
item.semiconductor-lab.camera.note3: In 1839, when Daguerre's process was announced, cameras with Chevalier's achromatic lens went on sale. Exposures at first took minutes and moving people did not register (which is why old street photos look empty).
item.semiconductor-lab.camera.note4: In 1840 Petzval built a bright lens designed by calculation, shortening exposures more than tenfold. Lens brightness (f-number) and plate sensitivity together set the exposure time. In lithography too, intensity times time (the dose) decides how the resist responds.
item.semiconductor-lab.camera.placeholde: Approximation: the right exposure is 60 s for silver plates and 1 s for dry plates (really several to 15 minutes for 1839 silver plates and about 1/25 s for dry plates around 1878). No picture of the scene (a photo holds place, time and exposure data; pictures come in the finishing phase).
item.semiconductor-lab.camera.hold: Hold a sensitized plate (silver plate or dry plate) in your other hand, then hold right-click with the camera
item.semiconductor-lab.exposed_plate.not: A plate that has seen light but shows nothing yet. Developing brings out the image.
A sensitized plate exposed in the camera. Develop it with mercury.
Where light fell there is an invisible 'latent image' (clusters of just a few silver atoms). Daguerre is said to have discovered by chance that mercury vapor makes it visible (⚠️ a tradition).
The latent image idea carries straight over to IC exposure: exposed resist looks unchanged, and the pattern appears only in the developer.
item.semiconductor-lab.developed_plate.n: A plate with a visible image. Light would still darken it, so it must be fixed.
Exposed plate + mercury (the iron flask comes back). Warm mercury vapor forms white amalgam grains where light fell, making the image. Fix with salt or hypo. ⚠ Mercury vapor is highly toxic.
Photographers of the time developed plates over heated mercury in a box, and many suffered mercury poisoning.
Amalgam grains scatter light and look white, while the mirror silver looks dark. Seen at some angles the image even reverses, so daguerreotypes were called 'the mirror with a memory'.
item.semiconductor-lab.daguerreotype.not: A photograph on a silver plate. There is only one in the world.

Developed plate + salt (Daguerre's way) or hypo. The tooltip shows where and when it was taken and the exposure. There is no negative, so it cannot be copied (negatives on gelatin dry plates [B-02b] allow many prints).
In 1839 the French government bought Daguerre's process and gave it to the world for free. Within a few years portraits were being taken all over the world.

Photography began 'copying patterns with light' and is the ancestor of IC photolithography (copying circuit patterns with light). Its ideas - sensitive layer, exposure, development, fixing - carried straight into semiconductor processing.
item.semiconductor-lab.exposed_dry_plate: A dry plate that has seen light in the camera. Nothing shows yet.
A photographic plate exposed in the camera (1 s in sun is right). Develop it with iron(II) sulfate developer.
In 1871 Maddox proposed plates of silver salts in gelatin, and by about 1878 factory-made dry plates were on sale. They kept for months and no longer had to be coated just before the picture.

History of exposure time: silver plate (1839) minutes to 15 min -> bromine sensitizing (1841) tens of seconds -> wet plate (1851) seconds -> gelatin dry plate (about 1878) about 1/25 s. Shutters became necessary and moving things could be frozen.
item.semiconductor-lab.developed_dry_pla: The image has appeared, with light and dark reversed. Not fixed yet.
Exposed dry plate + iron(II) sulfate. Silver salt where light fell turns into black silver grains. Fixing with hypo makes a negative.

A developer is a reducing agent that turns only the grains carrying a latent image into silver. Dry plates were developed with iron(II) sulfate or iron oxalate, later with organic developers such as hydroquinone.
IC exposure works the same way: exposed resist looks unchanged until the developer brings out the pattern.
item.semiconductor-lab.negative.note1: A glass plate with light and dark reversed. Printed on paper it gives as many normal pictures as you like.
item.semiconductor-lab.negative.note2: Developed dry plate + hypo (fixing). In the crafting grid, negative + printing paper -> print. The negative comes back with its photo data, so you can print again and again.
item.semiconductor-lab.negative.note3: Archer's wet plate of 1851 also gave glass negatives, but its collodion coating was flammable and dangerous, and plates had to be exposed and developed while still wet. Safe gelatin dry plates later replaced it.
item.semiconductor-lab.negative.note4: Printing many copies from one negative carried straight into photolithography: one photomask copies a circuit onto many wafers ([7-11]).
item.semiconductor-lab.negative.placehol: Approximation: the mod's emulsion is silver chloride (AgCl). Real dry plates used silver bromide (AgBr), which is far more sensitive (no bromine yet).
item.semiconductor-lab.printing_paper.no: Paper that darkens in light. Laid under a negative in the sun it becomes a photograph.
4 paper + salt + silver nitrate -> 4. Salted paper brushed with silver nitrate forms silver chloride in the paper. Combine with a negative to make a print.
Around 1840 Talbot made salted paper with table salt and silver nitrate and printed paper pictures from paper negatives (calotype). Albumen paper and gelatin papers followed.
Silver chloride paper shows the image just by long exposure to sunlight (printing-out). No developer is needed, but it takes time, and the print was fixed before display.
item.semiconductor-lab.printing_paper.pl: Approximation: no time in sunlight and no fixing of the print (prints are made in the crafting grid).
item.semiconductor-lab.print.note1: A photograph printed on paper from a negative. One negative can make any number.
item.semiconductor-lab.print.note2: Glass negative + printing paper (the negative returns). The tooltip shows where and when the negative was taken and its exposure.
item.semiconductor-lab.print.note3: With negatives, a photograph changed from a one-off object into something that could be handed out in many copies, which brought photographs into newspapers and books.
item.semiconductor-lab.print.note4: The negative reverses light and dark, and printing reverses it again. Photoresists likewise come as negative type (exposed parts stay) and positive type (exposed parts dissolve).
block.semiconductor-lab.carbide_lamp.not: A lamp that drips water on carbide, making a gas that burns brightly.

4 iron + soda-lime glass. Right-click with calcium carbide (A's [3-25]) and it shines at light level 15. It burns out in a few minutes. Adding carbide to a burnt-out lamp gives back the spent slaked lime. ⚠ Acetylene is a flammable gas (GHS).
CaC2 + 2H2O -> C2H2 + Ca(OH)2. The acetylene flame is very hot and its tiny soot particles glow strongly, giving a brilliant white light.

In 1892 Canadian-born Willson, trying to make aluminium, heated lime and coal in an arc furnace and made carbide by accident. In the early 20th century it lit miners' helmet lamps and bicycle and car headlights.
block.semiconductor-lab.carbide_lamp.pla: Approximation: filling with water is skipped (the lamp holds water).
message.semiconductor-lab.carbide_lamp.l: Water dripped onto the carbide and acetylene began to burn brightly
item.semiconductor-lab.nixie_tube.note1: A glass tube that lights up a glowing orange number.
item.semiconductor-lab.nixie_tube.note2: Neon in a glass tube, with ten metal cathodes shaped like 0-9 stacked behind a mesh anode. The chosen cathode glows with the neon light.
item.semiconductor-lab.nixie_tube.note3: Developed in the mid-1950s (Haydu Brothers, sold by Burroughs as the 'Nixie'). Sharp's first transistor calculator CS-10A (1964) showed its numbers on Nixie tubes. ⚠️ exact years not confirmed; the cathodes here are crude nickel.
item.semiconductor-lab.nixie_tube.note4: It needs about 170 V to glow, so calculators carried a high-voltage supply. LEDs and vacuum fluorescent displays replaced Nixies in the 1970s.
item.semiconductor-lab.key_switch.note1: A spring push-button. Calculators need one per key.
item.semiconductor-lab.key_switch.note2: Press to close two copper contacts, a steel spring pushes it back.
item.semiconductor-lab.key_switch.note3: Early calculators used mechanical key switches; the counter chip scanned them one after another to see which was pressed.
item.semiconductor-lab.key_switch.note4: Contacts 'bounce' for a few milliseconds when pressed, so circuits wait a moment before reading them (debouncing).
item.semiconductor-lab.calculator.note1: A calculator you built from your own chips. Right-click to add and subtract (4 digits).
item.semiconductor-lab.calculator.note2: Assembled from chips that passed the full adder, register and counter challenges, plus 14 keys, 4 Nixie tubes, a frame and wiring. Registers hold the numbers, the adder adds (subtracting = adding the complement), the counter reads the keys.
item.semiconductor-lab.calculator.note3: 1964 Sharp CS-10A: the first all-transistor desktop calculator, about 25 kg. From 1967 Texas Instruments built a hand-held IC calculator prototype; in 1971 Busicom asked Intel for calculator chips, which led to the 4004. ⚠️ the dates of IC calculators are approximate.
item.semiconductor-lab.calculator.note4: Only 4 digits, add and subtract (a game simplification). Overflow shows E; press C to clear, like real calculators.
item.semiconductor-lab.camera_module.not: A tiny camera that goes in a phone. You see the colour photo right after taking it.

2 camera lenses + IR-cut filter + colour image sensor + IC + dry cell. Right-click to take a photo (auto exposure; too dark is underexposed). Dry-plate cameras needed developing and fixing; this gives a photo at once.
In the 1990s CMOS image sensors became cheap and small, and from around 2000 mobile phones gained cameras. Today almost all photos in the world are taken with phone cameras.
With an F2 lens the diffraction blur for green light is about 2.7 um, larger than a ~1 um pixel, so adding pixels stops adding detail and image processing makes up the rest.
item.semiconductor-lab.camera_module.pla: Approximation: lens, pixel and F-number are typical values. A photo records place, time and exposure (no picture is drawn).
item.semiconductor-lab.camera_module.opt: F%s, %s um pixels, diffraction blur %s um (larger than a pixel = the lens limit)
item.semiconductor-lab.smartphone.note1: Calculator, photos and tilt in one device, built from your own chips (⚠️ cannot be assembled yet).
item.semiconductor-lab.smartphone.note2: A chip that passed the one-chip microcomputer, a camera, a MEMS accelerometer, a touch panel, a TFT LCD, a backlight and a lithium-ion battery on the assembly bench.
item.semiconductor-lab.smartphone.note3: iPhone 2007, Android 2008: phone, music, camera and internet in one device. The chips hold over a billion transistors (ArF immersion and multiple patterning).
item.semiconductor-lab.smartphone.note4: ⚠️ Placeholder: the TFT LCD [B-19] and white LED backlight [B-20] do not exist yet, so it cannot be assembled. The app screen's look awaits the user. Radio (calls, internet) is left out.
item.semiconductor-lab.smartphone.placeh: ⚠️ Placeholder: no TFT LCD or backlight yet (no screen)
message.semiconductor-lab.smartphone.pla: Smartphone: the screen (calculator, photos, tilt) is not built yet (waiting for the LCD, the backlight and a decision on the look)
item.semiconductor-lab.game_console.note: A table-tennis game built from your own chips. Right-click to play (move the left paddle with the mouse, first to 9 wins).
Chips that passed counter (2), full adder and register, plus knobs, wiring and a case, on the assembly bench. No CPU.
1972: the Magnavox Odyssey (the first home console, Ralph Baer) and Atari's Pong (arcade). Pong had no CPU: about 66 TTL chips counted the ball and paddle positions.

⚠️ The game runs in Java (your chips were proven by the challenges) and shows on screen instead of a TV. From the Atari 2600 (1977) and Famicom (1983), a CPU and cartridge ROM changed the game (a later stage).
item.semiconductor-lab.pva_film.note1: A clear thin film of a water-soluble plastic.
item.semiconductor-lab.pva_film.note2: Polyvinyl alcohol + water (bucket returned) -> 2. + iodine + potassium iodide + boric acid -> 2 polarizing films.
item.semiconductor-lab.pva_film.note3: Stretching the film lines up PVA's long chains in one direction. Iodine lining up along those chains is how a polarizer works.
item.semiconductor-lab.pva_film.note4: PVA is also used in laundry starch and in water-soluble film (detergent pods).
item.semiconductor-lab.pva_film.placehol: Approximation: really cast from solution and dried. The drying time is left out.
White crystals of potassium and iodine. They help iodine dissolve in water.
3 iodine + iron + potash (potassium carbonate) + water (bucket returned) -> 2. Used in the dye bath for polarizing film.

Iodine alone hardly dissolves in water, but with I- it forms I3- and dissolves. The old method made Fe3I8 from iron and iodine, then KI with potassium carbonate (the iron is left as black iron oxide).
Potassium iodide is also the 'stable iodine' tablet taken after nuclear accidents, to keep radioactive iodine from building up in the thyroid.
Approximation: the iron oxide and carbon dioxide left over are omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.polarizing_film.n: A film that only lets through light vibrating in one direction. Turn two of them and it goes dark.

PVA film + iodine + potassium iodide + boric acid -> 2. Experiment: hold one in each hand and right-click; the main-hand film turns 15 degrees each time and shows how much light gets through (50% when aligned, 0% at right angles). A part of liquid-crystal screens.

Stretching PVA film lines up its chains; dyed with iodine, the iodine forms thin rows (polyiodide) along them. Light vibrating along the rows is absorbed, light vibrating across them passes. Boric acid ties the chains together and fixes the order. With an angle θ between two films, brightness goes as cos²θ (Malus's law, 1809).

In 1929 Edwin Land made a sheet of tiny aligned crystals of iodoquinine (herapathite, Herapath 1852), and in 1938 the 'H-sheet' of iodine-dyed PVA. Today's LCD screens still carry this iodine-dyed film. Polarized sunglasses cut glare off water.
item.semiconductor-lab.polarizing_film.p: Approximation: calculated as an ideal film (a real one passes about 40%, and a little leaks even at right angles). The stretching step is merged into crafting.
message.semiconductor-lab.polarizing_fil: One polarizing film: %s%% of ordinary light gets through (hold another in your other hand to try two)
Angle between the two films %s degrees: brightness %s%% (Malus's law, cos²θ)
item.semiconductor-lab.arsenic.note1: Grey crystals. An LED material. Highly toxic. ⚠️ Skull symbol
item.semiconductor-lab.arsenic.note2: Compound furnace: white arsenic + coke → this. With gallium + red phosphorus → GaAsP wafers. Industrial material only.
item.semiconductor-lab.arsenic.note3: As2O3 + 3C → 2As + 3CO. Arsenic turns straight to vapour (sublimes, about 615 °C) and crystallises in the cool part. GHS: skull (acute toxicity), health hazard (carcinogen), environment.
item.semiconductor-lab.arsenic.note4: With gallium it forms the semiconductor gallium arsenide (GaAs), used in LEDs, lasers and phone radio amplifiers.
item.semiconductor-lab.gaasp_wafer.note1: A crystal of gallium, arsenic and phosphorus — a semiconductor that glows red when current flows.
item.semiconductor-lab.gaasp_wafer.note2: Compound furnace: gallium + arsenic + red phosphorus → 4. At a crafting table with zinc (makes p-type) + aluminium (contact) + glass (lens) → 4 red LEDs.
item.semiconductor-lab.gaasp_wafer.note3: GaAs alone gives invisible infrared. Adding phosphorus widens the step electrons fall across (band gap), turning the light red.
item.semiconductor-lab.gaasp_wafer.note4: In 1962 a GE researcher made the first visible-light LED (red) from GaAsP.
item.semiconductor-lab.gaasp_wafer.place: Omitted: ⚠️ real GaAsP is grown on a GaAs wafer from gases (arsine, phosphine, gallium chloride). Zinc diffusion is approximated at the crafting table.
item.semiconductor-lab.red_led.note1: A tiny part that glows red when current flows. It does not get hot like a bulb.
item.semiconductor-lab.red_led.note2: GaAsP wafer + zinc + aluminium + glass → 4 (crafting). 4 + glass + copper cable → LED lamp.
item.semiconductor-lab.red_led.note3: Current through the p-n junction makes electrons and holes meet and give off light with the energy of the gap — electricity straight to light.
item.semiconductor-lab.red_led.note4: The red digits of 1960s–70s calculators and watches were these red LEDs. ⚠️ White LEDs had to wait for the blue LED (from 1993).
block.semiconductor-lab.compound_furnace: A sealed furnace that frees arsenic and grows crystals of gallium, arsenic and phosphorus.
3 kW, 20 s each. ① white arsenic + coke → arsenic ② gallium + arsenic + red phosphorus → 4 GaAsP wafers (the polyethylene bottle pops out on top).
A closed quartz tube is heated so no toxic vapour escapes. ① is As2O3 + 3C → 2As + 3CO.
Arsenic is a poison, handled in closed equipment with exhaust treatment. ⚠️ Industrial material only.
Omitted: ⚠️ real GaAsP is grown by vapour-phase epitaxy (with toxic gases); solid materials stand in here. Power, time and amounts are game values.
block.semiconductor-lab.led_lamp.note1: A lamp of red LEDs. Glows on very little power.
block.semiconductor-lab.led_lamp.note2: Glows on 2 W (light level 7). Uses no materials. 4 red LEDs + 4 glass + copper cable (crafting).
block.semiconductor-lab.led_lamp.note3: A bulb heats a filament, so most of the power becomes heat. An LED turns electricity straight into light.
block.semiconductor-lab.led_lamp.note4: The 1962 red LED was very dim and used for indicator lamps. LEDs bright enough for lighting came much later.
block.semiconductor-lab.led_lamp.placeho: Omitted: ⚠️ brightness and power are game values (1962 LEDs were much dimmer).
item.semiconductor-lab.mbba.note1: A cloudy liquid that is a 'liquid crystal' at room temperature. The filling of an LCD.
item.semiconductor-lab.mbba.note2: Anisaldehyde + 4-butylaniline. With 2 rubbed ITO glass + 2 polarizing film + copper cable -> liquid-crystal cell.
item.semiconductor-lab.mbba.note3: N-(4-methoxybenzylidene)-4-butylaniline. Its long rod-shaped molecules line up even as a liquid (nematic liquid crystal, about 22-47 °C). In 1969 Kelker and Scheurle in Germany made it as a room-temperature liquid crystal.
item.semiconductor-lab.mbba.note4: MBBA broke down easily in moisture. In 1973 George Gray in Britain made the sturdy cyanobiphenyls (5CB and others), and LCD calculators and watches spread. Liquid crystals themselves were found by Reinitzer in 1888 in cholesteryl benzoate (two melting points).
item.semiconductor-lab.mbba.placeholder: Approximation: MBBA, whose prerequisites exist, instead of today's cyanobiphenyl or fluorinated mixtures.
Transparent electrode glass rubbed one way with cloth. It lines up the liquid crystal.
ITO glass + white wool (cloth). A material for the liquid-crystal cell (two pieces).

Rubbing the surface one way with cloth leaves invisible fine grooves that line the molecules up. Rubbing the top and bottom glass at 90 degrees to each other makes the molecules twist through 90 degrees.
In 1911 Mauguin in France found that rubbed surfaces align liquid crystals. Today a polyimide film is rubbed with cloth.
Approximation: really a polyimide film is rubbed. The cloth (wool) is used up.
block.semiconductor-lab.lcd_cell.note1: A window that turns dark when powered. One segment of an LCD.
block.semiconductor-lab.lcd_cell.note2: 2 rubbed ITO glass + MBBA + 2 polarizing film + copper cable. With power (1 W) through a copper cable the front goes dark; without, it is light. A calculator digit is seven of these segments.
block.semiconductor-lab.lcd_cell.note3: The two polarizers are at right angles. No voltage: the twisted liquid crystal turns the light by 90 degrees, so it passes the second film (light). Voltage: the molecules stand up along the field, the twist undoes, and the light is stopped (dark). Liquid crystals give no light themselves; they only open and close the light's path.
block.semiconductor-lab.lcd_cell.note4: In 1970-71 researchers at Roche in Switzerland published the TN mode (invented independently in the US at about the same time). In 1973 Sharp's EL-805 calculator used liquid crystal and CMOS for a thin calculator with long battery life. Real liquid crystals need only microwatts, so a watch runs for years on a battery.
block.semiconductor-lab.lcd_cell.placeho: Approximation: 1 W is a game value (real cells need microwatts). Real cells run on AC (DC would electrolyse the liquid crystal). Per-pixel transistors (TFT [B-19]) are not here yet.
item.semiconductor-lab.gan_wafer.note1: A crystal of gallium and nitrogen — a semiconductor that glows blue when current flows.
item.semiconductor-lab.gan_wafer.note2: Compound furnace: gallium + ammonia + magnesium → 4. At a crafting table with aluminium + glass → 4 blue LEDs.
item.semiconductor-lab.gan_wafer.note3: Gallium nitride has a wide band gap, giving blue light. Magnesium, which makes it p-type, only works after heat treatment — the discovery that made bright blue LEDs possible.
item.semiconductor-lab.gan_wafer.note4: Blue LEDs were long thought impossible; Japanese researchers made them practical with gallium nitride in the 1990s (Nobel Prize in Physics 2014).
item.semiconductor-lab.gan_wafer.placeho: Omitted: ⚠️ real GaN is grown on sapphire from a metal-organic gas (trimethylgallium) and ammonia (MOCVD). The buffer layer and heat treatment are omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.blue_led.note1: A tiny part that glows blue when current flows.
item.semiconductor-lab.blue_led.note2: GaN wafer + aluminium + glass → 4 (crafting). Add YAG phosphor for a white LED.
item.semiconductor-lab.blue_led.note3: Blue light has a shorter wavelength, so more energy, than red. With blue, the three primary colours of light were complete.
item.semiconductor-lab.blue_led.note4: Used in traffic lights, big screens and Blu-ray. ⚠️ Its developers are living, so no names are given.
item.semiconductor-lab.yag_phosphor.note: A powder that glows yellow under blue light. Material for white LEDs.
Compound furnace: yttrium oxide + alumina + cerium oxide → 4 (fired). With a blue LED → white LED.
Yttrium aluminium garnet (Y3Al5O12) with a little cerium; the cerium absorbs blue and emits yellow.
In 1996 a Japanese company put this phosphor on a blue LED and sold the first white LED.
item.semiconductor-lab.yag_phosphor.plac: Omitted: ⚠️ the real phosphor is fired at about 1500 °C with a flux. Amounts and mixing ratio are game values.
item.semiconductor-lab.white_led.note1: An LED that glows white — inside, a blue LED and a yellow-glowing powder.
item.semiconductor-lab.white_led.note2: Blue LED + YAG phosphor (crafting). 4 + glass + copper cable → white LED lamp; 3 + 3 glass + 2 polarising films + copper cable → backlight.
item.semiconductor-lab.white_led.note3: The phosphor turns some of the blue light yellow; blue and yellow together look white to the eye.
item.semiconductor-lab.white_led.note4: About 5–10 times as efficient as a bulb; today nearly all lighting and screen backlights are white LEDs.
item.semiconductor-lab.led_backlight.not: A light panel behind a liquid-crystal screen, which cannot glow on its own.
3 white LEDs + 3 glass (light guide) + 2 polarising films + copper cable (crafting). A smartphone part.
Light from white LEDs along the edge spreads through a clear plate and lights the whole screen evenly.
In the late 2000s white LEDs replaced cold-cathode fluorescent tubes (which contain mercury). ⚠️ Real light guides are acrylic.
item.semiconductor-lab.led_backlight.pla: Omitted: ⚠️ soda-lime glass stands in for the acrylic light guide.
block.semiconductor-lab.white_led_lamp.n: A bright white LED lamp that needs very little power.
Glows on 2 W (light level 15). 4 white LEDs + 4 glass + copper cable (crafting).
Most of the power becomes light, so it needs far less electricity than a bulb for the same brightness.
The 1996 white LED was dim, but efficiency rose and it became the main home light in the 2010s.
block.semiconductor-lab.white_led_lamp.p: Omitted: ⚠️ brightness and power are game values.
item.semiconductor-lab.tft_array_glass.n: Transparent-electrode glass coated with a thin silicon film that becomes a transistor for every pixel.
CVD furnace: ITO glass + silane cylinder + hydrogen → this (1–8). Becomes a TFT LCD at the assembly bench.
Breaking down silane in hydrogen gives hydrogenated amorphous (non-crystalline) silicon, so transistors can be made on large glass without a crystal wafer.
In 1979 Spear and LeComber at the University of Dundee showed TFTs of hydrogenated amorphous silicon.
item.semiconductor-lab.tft_array_glass.p: Omitted: ⚠️ the real film is made by plasma CVD (about 300 °C). The pixel pattern is not exposed or etched.
item.semiconductor-lab.tft_lcd.note1: A liquid-crystal screen with a transistor at every pixel. A smartphone part.
item.semiconductor-lab.tft_lcd.note2: Assembly bench: TFT array glass + rubbed ITO glass + MBBA (liquid crystal) + 2 polarising films + chip that passed NOT (driver). Held, it explains how it works in one line. A smartphone part (paired with the backlight).
item.semiconductor-lab.tft_lcd.note3: A plain TN panel fades earlier pixels while it writes many in turn. Each pixel's TFT holds its charge, keeping the brightness until the next update (active matrix).
item.semiconductor-lab.tft_lcd.note4: Brody and colleagues at Westinghouse showed an LCD with a TFT per pixel in 1973–74; Sharp announced a 14-inch colour TFT LCD in 1988.
item.semiconductor-lab.tft_lcd.placehold: Omitted: ⚠️ no pixel pattern or colour filters, and no picture (explanation only).
item.semiconductor-lab.tft_lcd.holding: Each pixel's TFT holds its charge until the next update (active matrix)
